intro: Richard Strauss’s tone poem Don Juan, Op. 20, opens with a rising figure in the violins in E major and ends in E minor. Albert Coates conducted this acoustic recording in 1922. It was first issued on four sides of two records.

sections.label: A · The violins leap upwards
sections.mNote: A fast flourish launches the E-major theme

sections.label: B · Solo violin, then orchestral melody
sections.mNote: A solo violin line leads to a full orchestral melody.

sections.label: C · Oboe melody over muted strings
sections.mNote: The oboe plays a long melody over muted strings.

sections.label: Dev · Four horns and running figures
sections.mNote: The horn theme is combined with the opening theme.

sections.label: Link · Harp tremolos and strings near the bridge
sections.mNote: Quiet recollections over a trembling accompaniment

sections.label: A′ · The E-major theme returns
sections.mNote: The violins climb again; the horn call enters after them.

sections.label: Coda · Trumpet enters after a silence
sections.mNote: Trembling strings take the music into E minor.

cues.title: Opening flourish and violin theme
cues.text: A flourish opens Don Juan in E major. The violins’ theme climbs in long, accented strides, with quick notes running between them.
cues.evidence: Gerald Larner describes the opening flourish and ascending E-major violin theme. Instrumental descriptions here follow Strauss’s orchestral score. https://geraldlarner.com/work/strauss-richard-don-juan-tone-poem-op-20
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Lenau extracts printed with the score
cues.text: Strauss printed three extracts from Nikolaus Lenau’s verse drama before the score. In them Don Juan pursues a love that no single encounter can satisfy. The last extract describes the world around him as empty and dark.
cues.evidence: Larner discusses and quotes the three Lenau extracts printed with the score. The Richard Strauss Edition introduction confirms Strauss’s explicit allegiance to Lenau. https://geraldlarner.com/work/strauss-richard-don-juan-tone-poem-op-20

cues.title: Padua and first sketches, 1888
cues.text: Strauss later recalled that the first themes came to him in Padua, in the cloister of Sant’Antonio, during a holiday in May 1888. His sketches show that he had begun months earlier. On his twenty-fourth birthday, 11 June, he told his uncle that he had “drafted a single-movement Don Juan”.
cues.evidence: Walter Werbeck’s introduction to the Richard Strauss Edition (p. XII) gives Strauss’s later recollection of Padua, the Italian holiday of 16 May to 10 June 1888, the sketches pointing to a start in about January 1888, and the letter to his uncle Carl Hörburger of 11 June 1888. https://schott-production.s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com/public_content/element/321495/dl/don_juan_einleitung_introduction.pdf

cues.title: First love scene, solo violin
cues.text: The first love scene opens with a solo violin. The melody then passes through the orchestra and expands, until Don Juan’s upward-rushing theme interrupts it.
cues.evidence: Larner’s score account traces the solo violin, the expansion of the first love theme and the main theme’s interruption. https://geraldlarner.com/work/strauss-richard-don-juan-tone-poem-op-20
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Letter to his father, 1889
cues.text: At the Weimar rehearsals the horn and trumpet players blew themselves “blue in the face”. Strauss told his father so on 8 November 1889, delighted with the sound. Three days later he conducted the première.
cues.evidence: Strauss to his father, 8 November 1889, Briefe an die Eltern 1882–1906, edited by Willi Schuh (1954), pp. 119–120. English translation and première date in the Richard Strauss Edition introduction, pp. XIV–XV. https://schott-production.s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com/public_content/element/321495/dl/don_juan_einleitung_introduction.pdf

cues.title: Hans von Bülow, 1888–1890
cues.text: In 1888 Hans von Bülow, Strauss’s mentor, rejected Macbeth, and Strauss wrote that Don Juan might soon join it in his desk. Bülow heard Don Juan with an orchestra at a Berlin rehearsal in January 1890 and sent Strauss a card praising the “magnificent” work.
cues.evidence: Richard Strauss Edition introduction, pp. XIII–XIV: Strauss’s letter of 24 August 1888 (“Don Juan will perhaps soon come to keep it company”), the Berlin rehearsal of 13 January 1890 and Bülow’s card, quoted in footnote 17. https://schott-production.s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com/public_content/element/321495/dl/don_juan_einleitung_introduction.pdf

cues.title: Victor 55176 and 55177
cues.text: Coates’s performance was issued on two twelve-inch, 78 rpm Victor records, numbered 55176 and 55177. The music took four sides. At home, a listener had to lift the needle and turn the disc, then change to the second record.
cues.evidence: The Animating Apothecary transfer identifies the two twelve-inch, 78 rpm Victor discs and joins their four sides. https://archive.org/details/1922-don-juan-richard-strauss-albert-coates-and-victor-symphony-vic-55176-77-4-sides

cues.title: Completion of the score, 1888
cues.text: On the last page of his score Strauss wrote: “begun in the middle of June, completed 30 September 1888”. It was his second tone poem, and he was twenty-four. Neither it nor Macbeth had yet been performed, and the first performance was more than a year away.
cues.evidence: Richard Strauss Edition introduction, p. XIII: the inscription on the last page of the score copy, the completion on 30 September 1888 and the state of his unperformed tone poems. https://schott-production.s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com/public_content/element/321495/dl/don_juan_einleitung_introduction.pdf

cues.title: Oboe melody with muted strings
cues.text: A serenade in the lower strings and answering phrases in the flute lead to a long melody for the oboe. Strauss accompanies it with muted strings.
cues.evidence: Larner describes the lower-string serenade, flute answers and oboe melody. Strauss’s letter of 8 November 1889 singles out the muted accompaniment in bars 232–307; Richard Strauss Edition introduction, p. XV.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Dedication to Ludwig Thuille, 1889
cues.text: Strauss dedicated Don Juan to Ludwig Thuille, who received the score in July 1889. Strauss dedicated each of his first four tone poems to a member of the Munich circle around Alexander Ritter. Macbeth went to Ritter, Don Juan to Thuille, Death and Transfiguration to Friedrich Rösch and Till Eulenspiegel to Arthur Seidl.
cues.evidence: Richard Strauss Edition introduction, pp. XI and XIV: the four dedications to members of Ritter’s circle and Thuille’s receipt of the score in July 1889. https://schott-production.s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com/public_content/element/321495/dl/don_juan_einleitung_introduction.pdf

cues.title: First performance, Weimar, 1889
cues.text: Strauss conducted the première on 11 November 1889, two months after taking up his post at Weimar. He told his father that it “sounded enchanting” and had won a storm of applause nearly unheard of in Weimar. The Musikalisches Wochenblatt reported three curtain calls.
cues.evidence: Richard Strauss Edition introduction, pp. XIV–XV: Strauss’s start at Weimar on 9 September 1889, the première on 11 November 1889, his report to his father and the Musikalisches Wochenblatt review. https://schott-production.s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com/public_content/element/321495/dl/don_juan_einleitung_introduction.pdf

cues.title: Horn theme in unison
cues.text: Four horns play a broad theme in unison. In the development it is combined with the opening theme, while quick figures run around the longer melodic lines. The horn theme returns at the final climax.
cues.evidence: Gerald Larner and Herbert Glass describe the unison horn call, its role in the development and its later return. https://geraldlarner.com/work/strauss-richard-don-juan-tone-poem-op-20; https://www.laphil.com/works/don-juan
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Hanslick’s review, Vienna, 1892
cues.text: In January 1892 Eduard Hanslick reviewed the Vienna Philharmonic’s Don Juan in the Neue Freie Presse. Of the younger composers he wrote: “Colour is everything to them, musical thought nothing,” He said young Wagnerians recalled the piece with a “voluptuous shiver”, and called it “a tumult of dazzling blots of colour”.
cues.evidence: Eduard Hanslick, Neue Freie Presse, Vienna, 12 January 1892 (Nr. 9835), on the Philharmonic concert of the previous Sunday: “Die Farbe ist ihnen Alles, der musikalische Gedanke nichts”; “Wagner-Jünglinge … ein wollüstiger Schauer über den Rücken”; “ein Tumult von blendenden Farbenklecksen”. Our translations. Hanslick Online, Austrian Academy of Sciences: https://hanslick.acdh.oeaw.ac.at/c__1892.01.12.html

cues.title: The “hangover passage”, bars 447–457
cues.text: Strauss called this the “hangover passage” in a letter to his father of 8 November 1889. In bars 447–457 the harp plays trembling chords (bisbigliando). The violas and second violins play sul ponticello, close to the bridge.
cues.evidence: Strauss to his father, 8 November 1889, Briefe an die Eltern, pp. 119–120; Richard Strauss Edition introduction, p. XV, identifies harp bisbigliando and viola and second-violin sul ponticello at bars 447–457.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Recapitulation in E major
cues.text: The main theme returns in E major, with the violins climbing again. The horn call returns and joins the final drive. The music continues past the point of a triumphant ending, towards the sudden break.
cues.evidence: Larner identifies the E-major recapitulation, the horn call’s return and the continued drive towards the sudden break. https://geraldlarner.com/work/strauss-richard-don-juan-tone-poem-op-20
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Recording at Hayes, 1922
cues.text: The orchestra was the Gramophone Company’s own Symphony Orchestra. Albert Coates conducted it in Room 1 of the company’s studio at Hayes, Middlesex, where the first part was made on 28 April 1922, and take three was kept. Victor issued the set in America as 55176–77.
cues.evidence: DAHR matrix Cc1260 (Don Juan, Part 1): Symphony Orchestra [Gramophone Co.], Albert Coates, 28 April 1922, Hayes, Middlesex, Room 1, takes 1–3 with take 3 as master, issued on Gramophone D-670 and Victor 55176: https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/matrix/detail/2000007287/Cc1260-Don_Juan. The Victor 55176–77 set: https://archive.org/details/1922-don-juan-richard-strauss-albert-coates-and-victor-symphony-vic-55176-77-4-sides

cues.title: Coda in E minor
cues.text: A sudden silence stops the music. A dissonant trumpet note sounds over a wind chord, and the violins play tremolando beneath it. E major turns to E minor for the close.
cues.evidence: Larner describes the silence, wind chords, dissonant trumpet, tremolando violins and E-minor close. https://geraldlarner.com/work/strauss-richard-don-juan-tone-poem-op-20
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Solo violin leads to the love theme
transitions.to: B · Solo violin, then orchestral melody
transitions.how: An expressive melody first breaks into the rush at fortissimo. The orchestra then thins out for a solo violin, whose phrases prepare the full statement of that melody. The first love theme is then stated in full and expanded by the orchestra.
transitions.evidence: Gerald Larner’s score account gives the fortissimo announcement, solo-violin preparation and expansion of the first love theme. https://geraldlarner.com/work/strauss-richard-don-juan-tone-poem-op-20

transitions.title: Viola and cello serenade to oboe
transitions.from: B · Solo violin, then orchestral melody
transitions.to: C · Oboe melody over muted strings
transitions.how: The upward-rushing theme interrupts the first love scene. In the next section violas and cellos begin a serenade, and the flute follows. The oboe then takes over the long melody above muted strings, in bars 232–307.
transitions.evidence: Larner traces the intervening main theme, low-string serenade, flute and oboe. The Richard Strauss Edition introduction, p. XV, identifies the muted oboe passage as bars 232–307.

transitions.title: Oboe love scene to horn call
transitions.from: C · Oboe melody over muted strings
transitions.to: Dev · Four horns and running figures
transitions.how: A broad unison call for four horns, marked sehr energisch, carries Don Juan away from the oboe’s love scene. In the development the call is paired with the opening theme, and quick orchestral figures surround these two large ideas.
transitions.evidence: Larner describes the horn call’s emergence and role in the development; Herbert Glass gives sehr energisch and the four horns in unison. https://www.laphil.com/works/don-juan

transitions.title: Harp bisbigliando and strings sul ponticello
transitions.from: Dev · Four horns and running figures
transitions.to: Link · Harp tremolos and strings near the bridge
transitions.how: Near the end of the development the driven middle section gives way to quiet recollections of the love music. In bars 447–457 Strauss writes bisbigliando chords for the harp, and the violas and second violins play sul ponticello, bowing close to the bridge. The remembered melodies sound above this thin accompaniment.
transitions.evidence: Larner identifies the quiet recollections near the end of the development. Richard Strauss Edition introduction, p. XV, specifies harp bisbigliando and strings sul ponticello in bars 447–457.

transitions.title: The violins return to E major
transitions.from: Link · Harp tremolos and strings near the bridge
transitions.how: The quiet recollections lead into the main theme in E major. The violins restore their upward leaps and the orchestra builds up behind them. The horn call returns later in the closing climax, so the work’s two most forceful themes both appear in its closing stretch.
transitions.evidence: Gerald Larner’s account identifies the E-major recapitulation and the horn call in the closing climax.

transitions.title: Silence, then a dissonant trumpet
transitions.to: Coda · Trumpet enters after a silence
transitions.how: The rushing music breaks off. After the silence the wind enter with chords, a dissonant trumpet note sounds against them, and the violins continue in tremolo. E remains the tonic, but the harmony turns to E minor for the close.
transitions.evidence: Gerald Larner describes the final silence, wind chord, trumpet dissonance, string tremolo and E-minor close. https://geraldlarner.com/work/strauss-richard-don-juan-tone-poem-op-20

composer.epithet: Composer, the son of a horn player, who wrote long farewell songs for soprano.
facts: Munich, with Friedrich Wilhelm Meyer; conducting with Hans von Bülow at Meiningen
Munich · Weimar · Berlin Court Opera, 1898–1918 · Vienna State Opera, 1919–24
Tone poems, fifteen operas, two horn concertos and more than two hundred songs
composer.background:
Richard Strauss grew up hearing the horn. His father Franz played in the Munich Court Orchestra, including the first performances of Wagner’s Tristan and Die Meistersinger, and detested the music. At home, Mozart was placed above every other composer, and Haydn and Beethoven were also approved. Richard, born in 1864, had piano lessons from the age of four and was composing at six. His mother Josepha came from the Pschorr brewing family. He studied privately with Friedrich Wilhelm Meyer and learnt how an orchestra sounds from the players who worked beside his father.

Hans von Bülow took him to Meiningen in 1885. At twenty-one he had an orchestra of his own to rehearse, as well as a choir and a princess to teach. The violinist Alexander Ritter, married to Wagner’s niece, completed his conversion to the music his father disliked. Ritter also urged Liszt’s symphonic poems upon him. Strauss spent the next decade writing for the concert orchestra without voices.
